title: Fallacies of presumption and ambiguity
note: Fallacies of presumption smuggle in an unearned assumption: that only two options exist, that the conclusion is already true, or that a few cases speak for all. Fallacies of ambiguity exploit a word or sentence with more than one meaning, or carry a property from parts to whole, or whole to parts, without warrant.

read.title: Hidden assumptions, shifting words
text: Some arguments go wrong not because a premise is irrelevant but because they quietly presume something unearned. A false dilemma presents two options as the only ones: love your country or leave it, as if criticizing it from within were impossible. Begging the question assumes what it sets out to prove, as when someone trusts a man because the man says he is trustworthy. A loaded question such as 'Have you stopped cheating?' traps any direct answer in an assumption. A hasty generalization treats a handful of cases as a rule.

Other fallacies trade on ambiguity. Equivocation shifts a word's meaning between premises: nothing beats love, a sandwich beats nothing, so a sandwich beats love. Amphiboly arises from grammar rather than a single word, as in 'I saw the man with the telescope'. Composition moves a property from parts to whole, as when a team of stars is assumed to be a great team; division moves it from whole to parts.
The cure in each case is the same: state the hidden assumption or the two meanings out loud. Once it is visible, you can ask whether it is true.

q.q: What makes 'Have you stopped cheating?' fallacious?
o: Any direct answer accepts a hidden assumption
It uses a word in two senses

q.q: How does amphiboly differ from equivocation, per the reading?
o: Amphiboly comes from grammar, not one word's two meanings

q.q: What cure does the reading recommend?
o: State the hidden assumption or meanings out loud
